rubric.why: Identifies the subject matter of chemistry.
rubric.description: States that chemistry is the study of matter.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying matter as the subject of chemistry.

rubric.why: Includes key aspects studied in chemistry.
rubric.description: Mentions aspects such as the composition, structure, properties or changes of matter.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning at least two relevant aspects.

modelAnswer: Chemistry is the branch of science that studies the composition, structure and properties of matter and the changes it undergoes.

items.followUp: Define molecular formula with an example.

rubric.why: An empirical formula expresses the simplest ratio of atoms.
rubric.description: Defines an empirical formula as showing the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it gives the simplest ratio of atoms.

rubric.why: A correct example demonstrates the definition.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example, such as CH₂O for glucose or CH for benzene.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid empirical formula example.

modelAnswer: An empirical formula shows the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.
For example, the empirical formula of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, is CH₂O.

items.followUp: State two properties of cathode rays.

rubric.why: Positive charge is a defining property of positive rays.
rubric.description: States that positive rays consist of positively charged particles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying their positive charge.

rubric.why: Any one accepted behaviour or path is a valid second property.
rubric.description: Gives another property, such as travelling in straight lines, passing through perforations in the cathode, or being deflected by electric or magnetic fields.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct additional property.

modelAnswer: Positive rays are streams of positively charged particles.
They travel in straight lines and can pass through perforations in the cathode.

items.followUp: Why are noble gases generally chemically stable?

rubric.why: Their outer electron shell is complete.
rubric.description: States that noble gases have a complete outermost (valence) electron shell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the full outer shell.

rubric.why: A complete outer shell explains their low tendency to react.
rubric.description: Explains that they have little tendency to gain, lose or share electrons, so they are unreactive.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the complete shell to stability or low reactivity.

modelAnswer: Noble gases have completely filled outermost electron shells.
Therefore, they have little tendency to gain, lose or share electrons and are generally unreactive.

items.followUp: State the octet rule and give one example of an atom that follows it.

rubric.why: The duplet rule concerns a stable outer shell containing two electrons.
rubric.description: Defines the duplet rule as attaining two electrons in the outermost shell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct two-electron definition.

rubric.why: The octet rule concerns a stable outer shell containing eight electrons.
rubric.description: Defines the octet rule as attaining eight electrons in the outermost shell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct eight-electron definition.

modelAnswer: The duplet rule states that an atom becomes stable when it has two electrons in its outermost shell.
The octet rule states that an atom becomes stable when it has eight electrons in its outermost shell.

items.followUp: Explain the difference between a single covalent bond and a triple covalent bond.

rubric.why: A single covalent bond involves one shared pair of electrons.
rubric.description: States that a single covalent bond consists of one shared pair of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying one shared electron pair.

rubric.why: A double covalent bond involves two shared pairs of electrons.
rubric.description: States that a double covalent bond consists of two shared pairs of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying two shared electron pairs.

modelAnswer: A single covalent bond is formed when two atoms share one pair of electrons.
A double covalent bond is formed when two atoms share two pairs of electrons.

items.followUp: Define diffusion of gases and give an example.

rubric.why: Effusion involves gas passing through a very small opening.
rubric.description: Defines effusion as the escape of gas molecules through a tiny hole.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying escape through a tiny opening.

rubric.why: An example should illustrate gas escaping through a small opening.
rubric.description: Gives a relevant example, such as gas escaping through a pinhole in a container or balloon.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid example of gas escaping through a small opening.

modelAnswer: Effusion is the escape of gas molecules through a tiny hole in a container.
For example, gas escaping through a pinhole in a balloon is effusion.

items.followUp: Name the two crystalline allotropes of carbon.

rubric.why: Rhombic sulphur is one of the two common crystalline allotropes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming rhombic sulphur.

rubric.why: Monoclinic sulphur is the other common crystalline allotrope.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming monoclinic sulphur.

modelAnswer: The two allotropic forms of sulphur are rhombic sulphur and monoclinic sulphur.
